findings.claim: Deletes by user id, so a used token **still works**
findings.evidence: resetTokens is keyed by token, so delete(row.userId) removes nothing; redeeming the same token twice succeeds (ran it).

findings.claim: The reset token is written to the log
findings.evidence: console.log prints the full token; anyone who reads the logs can reset that user's password for 15 minutes.

findings.claim: `validPassword` returns an error message, not a boolean
findings.evidence: It returns null for a good password and a string for a bad one, so `if (validPassword(p))` reads backwards.

scenes.narration: Users who forget their password can now reset it. The service mails a one time token that is good for fifteen minutes, and the token lets the user set a new password.
scenes.summary: Reset a forgotten password with a one-time token
bullets: A used token must stop working
The token is a secret: nothing may log it
A weak new password is refused

scenes.narration: Two new modules hold the logic. The routes file adds two addresses the app can call. One new test file covers the normal reset and two refusals.
A reset takes two requests. The first asks for a token, and the second uses it.

steps.say: First the user asks for a reset. The handler creates a token, stores it with its expiry, and mails a link.
Then the link sends the token with a new password. The token is checked, the password is set, and the token should be thrown away.

scenes.narration: A reset token has three states. A token starts as issued, and ends either used or expired. Neither end lets the token work again.
This is the endpoint that starts a reset.

steps.say: The endpoint looks up the user. An unknown user gets the same accepted answer, so nobody can learn which accounts exist.
Then the endpoint makes a reset token. I think the logging line is risky. The log gets the whole token, and anyone who holds that token can change the user's password.
Finally it emails the reset link to the user and answers that the request was accepted.

scenes.narration: The reset module makes the token.

steps.say: A token lives for fifteen minutes.
The token is thirty two random bytes, written out as text. The token is stored with its user and the time it runs out.

scenes.narration: Using a token sets the new password.

steps.say: A token that is unknown, or that has run out, is refused.
A new password that breaks the rules is refused, with the reason.
Then the user's password is changed.

steps.note: deletes by user id, not token
steps.say: I think this delete is a bug. Tokens are stored under the token itself, but the delete looks them up by the user's id, so nothing gets deleted. I tried it, and the same reset link worked a second time.

scenes.narration: The password rules live in their own module.

steps.note: returns an error, not a yes or no
steps.say: A small one. I think the function's name sounds like a yes or no answer. But the function gives back the reason a password is refused, or nothing when the password is fine.
A password must be text, at least twelve characters long, and contain a digit.

scenes.narration: Three new tests cover the reset. None of them uses a token twice, which is why the reuse bug still passes.

cases.proves: a valid token changes the password

cases.proves: a token is refused at its expiry time

gaps: The mailer failing after the token is stored

scenes.narration: To recap, I flagged one bug, one risk and one small issue. Fix the token reuse first, because a used reset link can change the password again.
